title: When "Not a Culture Fit" Really Means "Not Like Us"
summary: Culture fit sounds careful, but in a well-known study it mostly meant "similar to me." How to turn a vague hunch into named behaviors you can check, and what to hire for.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The candidate has just left. The system design round went well: clear trade-offs, honest about what they didn't know, sharp questions back. Then someone in the debrief leans back and says, "Strong technically. Not sure about culture fit, though."

The room nods. Nobody asks what that means. And because nobody asks, that one sentence ends up weighing more than anything the candidate said in the past hour.

Culture does matter. Nobody wants to hire a strong engineer who then humiliates juniors in code review or hides mistakes during incidents. The trouble is that "culture fit" is vague enough to mean that, and also vague enough to mean "they didn't laugh at our jokes."

What "fit" turns out to mean

Sociologist Lauren Rivera studied this up close. She interviewed 120 people who hire for elite U.S. investment banks, law firms and consulting firms, and sat in on a hiring committee (Rivera, "Hiring as Cultural Matching," American Sociological Review, 2012). Evaluators wanted candidates who were competent and also culturally similar to themselves: similar hobbies, experiences and ways of presenting themselves. More than half said fit was their most important criterion at the interview stage, rating it above analytical thinking and communication. Roughly four in five used some version of the "airport test": would I want to be stuck in an airport in a snowstorm with this person?

Those firms aren't software teams, and Rivera notes that how much similarity counts may vary by occupation. Still, the airport test will sound familiar to anyone who has sat in an engineering debrief. It tells you whether the interviewer would enjoy dinner with someone. It says very little about how that person behaves when production is down at 2 a.m.

Why a vague verdict is a problem

Compare two reasons to say no. "They missed the failure modes in the queue design and never sized the database" can be checked. Someone can say "they covered that in the last ten minutes," and the panel can look at the notes. "Not a culture fit" can't be checked. It ends the discussion and hides whatever sat behind it, a fair concern or a bias.

Small signals slip in this way. A candidate who talks slowly gets read as low energy. One who asks a lot of careful questions comes across as unsure. Someone from a company with different habits doesn't know your team's shorthand, so their answers feel less sharp. None of that tells you whether they'll be kind in review, honest in an incident or generous with context, and those are the parts of culture you live with every day.

Name the behavior before the interview

The fix is to decide which behaviors you're looking for before you meet anyone, and write them down. Google's re:Work guide on structured interviewing says it plainly: instead of relying on gut feel or vague cultural fit, focus on tangible areas. Ask every candidate for the role the same kinds of questions, and describe in advance what a poor, borderline, solid and outstanding answer covers (re:Work: A guide to structured interviewing). The guide reports that structured interviews predict better and show smaller score differences between demographic groups. The same discipline helps when you weigh potential against experience.

For culture, it can look like this:

What the team says it values What you'd see One way to check in an interview
"We give direct feedback" They name a problem clearly and without contempt "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate's design. What did you say, and how did it land?"
"We own our incidents" They describe their own part in a failure without shifting blame "Walk me through a production issue you were involved in. What would you do differently?"
"We handle ambiguity well" They break a fuzzy problem into decisions and questions Give a vague requirement and notice which questions they ask first
"We're good to newer people" They explain without talking down Ask them to explain a past project as if to someone who just joined

Atlassian went down this road years ago. In a 2018 post it explained that it had stopped interviewing for culture fit, because that tends to produce teams that look like the interviewers, and now checks values alignment with structured questions about specific behavior (Atlassian: Hire for values). Two details are worth copying. The values interviewers are trained, picked to be balanced across demographics, roles and locations, and don't need to know the candidate's job. And the post warns that generic values like "excellence" are hollow and can be used as a weapon.

Real red flags still count

None of this means every difference is welcome. Some behavior hurts a team however strong the code is: brushing off product context, humiliating juniors, refusing review, hunting for someone to blame after an incident. Atlassian treats a values mismatch as a veto, and you can too. Just name it. "They blamed two former teammates for the outage and never mentioned their own part" is a reason the whole panel can weigh. "Not a fit" gives the panel nothing to weigh.

Ask what the team is missing

A more useful question than "do they fit?" is "what would they add?" A team already has plenty of itself. It might need someone who asks the slower question, writes clearer docs, notices the teammate who hasn't spoken yet, or brings habits from a very different company. That person may not feel like an easy fit at first, and they may bring a bit of friction. A healthy team can tell friction that helps it see something true from friction that does real harm.

Engineers already know this from code. A codebase built only from familiar patterns can turn fragile when nobody questions the assumptions underneath. Teams work the same way.

Four questions for the next debrief

When someone says "not a culture fit," you don't need to argue. Ask:

  1. What exactly did you see or hear?
  2. Which of our written values or behaviors does it touch?
  3. Is this about behavior, or about style?
  4. If a candidate from a background more familiar to us did the same thing, would we describe it the same way?

Sometimes the answer is a real concern that now has a name. Sometimes the concern fades halfway through. Either way, the decision gets better.

Before your next hiring loop

  • Write down three to five behaviors that make up your team's culture, in plain words.
  • For each one, pick an interview question and describe what a solid answer sounds like.
  • Take "culture fit" off the scorecard and put the named behaviors there instead.
  • In the debrief, ask the four questions above whenever a verdict sounds like a feeling.

faqs.q: What is wrong with hiring for culture fit?
faqs.a: The phrase is vague enough to mean "similar to us." In Lauren Rivera's 2012 study of elite U.S. banks, law firms and consulting firms, evaluators looked for candidates who shared their hobbies, experiences and self-presentation, and more than half ranked fit as their top criterion at the interview stage.

faqs.q: What should we assess instead of culture fit?
faqs.a: Write down the specific behaviors your team values, such as giving direct feedback or owning incidents, and check each one with a structured question and a rubric. Google's re:Work guide recommends tangible focus areas over gut feel or vague cultural fit.

faqs.q: What is culture add or culture contribution?
faqs.a: It means asking what a candidate would bring that the team lacks, such as clearer writing, slower questions or experience from a different kind of company. It still requires shared values like honesty and respect.

faqs.q: Can we still reject someone over behavior?
faqs.a: Yes. Atlassian treats a values mismatch as a veto. The difference is naming the behavior, for example blaming teammates for an outage, so the whole panel can weigh it.
